client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really guilty because my partner keeps saying I’m distant and unavailable. I’ve been working late almost every night, and I know it’s affecting our relationship, but I’m scared if I pull back at work, I’ll fall behind or disappoint my boss. I’m not sure if therapy can even help me fix this—it feels like I’m stuck between two impossible choices.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of guilt and pressure, torn between your relationship and work responsibilities. That must feel overwhelming, especially when it seems like no matter what you do, someone might be let down. What do you think is the most immediate fear driving these feelings—disappointing your partner, your boss, or perhaps yourself?

client: I think my biggest fear is disappointing my partner because I know how much they’re hurting. But at the same time, I’m terrified of letting my boss down—I feel like if I don’t keep up this pace, I’ll lose their trust or even my job. It’s like I’m stuck in this cycle where I can’t win no matter what I do. I don’t know how to balance both without feeling like I’m failing one or the other.
therapist: I hear how trapped you feel between these two important parts of your life—it’s understandable that this balancing act would leave you exhausted and fearful. When you think about these fears of disappointing others, what happens if you imagine *your own* needs in this equation? Where do they fit in this balance?

client: Honestly, I don’t even think about my own needs much—it feels selfish somehow. If I focus on myself, I worry I’ll just make things worse for my partner or my boss. It’s like I’ve convinced myself that my needs don’t matter compared to theirs. But I know I’m exhausted, and deep down, I feel like I’m losing myself in all of this. It’s just hard to see how I can prioritize myself without feeling like I’m abandoning everyone else.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a heavy burden, putting everyone else’s needs before your own, and that’s left you feeling drained and disconnected from yourself. That sense of guilt about prioritizing your own well-being is understandable, but it’s also keeping you stuck in this cycle. What do you think might happen if you started to see your own needs as equally important to those of your partner and boss?

client: I guess if I started seeing my own needs as important, it might take some of the pressure off, but I’m worried it would just create new problems. Like, what if my partner thinks I’m being selfish, or my boss thinks I’m slacking? It feels risky to even consider it. I’m not sure how to make that shift without feeling like I’m letting people down or causing conflict.
therapist: It sounds like you’re stuck in a cycle where prioritizing yourself feels risky, almost like it could lead to conflict or disappointment from others. That fear of being seen as selfish or slacking is understandable, but it’s also keeping you from finding a healthier balance. What would it feel like to take one small step—like setting aside even a little time for yourself—to see how it might shift things, both for you and for others?

client: I guess I could try taking a small step, like maybe leaving work on time one day a week, but I’m still worried it’ll backfire. What if my boss notices and starts questioning my commitment? Or what if my partner still feels like it’s not enough? It feels like even a small change could make things worse instead of better. I’m not sure I’m ready to risk that yet.
therapist: It sounds like even considering that small step brings up a lot of "what ifs"—your mind is warning you of all the ways this could go wrong, and that makes it hard to take action. That hesitation is completely normal when we're trying to break out of a familiar (even if painful) pattern. What would help you feel a little more secure in testing this out—maybe preparing what to say to your boss, or checking in with your partner first about what would feel meaningful to them?

client: I guess preparing what to say to my boss or checking in with my partner first might help, but it still feels like I’m walking on eggshells. What if I try to explain leaving on time to my boss, and they still judge me for it? Or what if my partner says they need more than just one evening a week? It feels like no matter what I do, I’ll fall short. I’m not sure I can handle the disappointment if it doesn’t go well.
therapist: It sounds like even with preparation, there’s still a deep fear of falling short—like any step forward could lead to disappointment, and that feels paralyzing. That fear is so real, but I wonder if we could explore what it would mean if things *didn’t* go perfectly? What if, for now, the goal wasn’t about getting it exactly right, but just noticing what happens when you try something small?

client: I guess I could try noticing what happens instead of expecting perfection, but it’s hard to let go of that pressure. I feel like I’ve always had to get things exactly right, or else I’m failing. It’s scary to think about just experimenting with this and seeing how it goes—what if I feel even worse if it doesn’t work out? I’m not sure I’m ready to face that possibility yet.
therapist: That pressure to get everything exactly right—to avoid "failing" at all costs—sounds like it’s been weighing on you for a long time. It makes sense that trying something new, especially when it feels uncertain, would bring up so much fear. What do you think it would take for you to feel just a little more grounded in this experiment, even if it doesn’t go perfectly?

client: I think it would help if I had some kind of backup plan—like, if leaving work on time one day doesn’t go well, I could have a way to address it without feeling like I’ve completely failed. But even then, I’m worried I’ll overthink it and make things worse. It’s hard to imagine feeling grounded when I’m constantly second-guessing myself.
therapist: Having a backup plan sounds like a thoughtful way to ease into this—it’s understandable that you’d want some reassurance before trying something new. It’s okay to feel uncertain and second-guess yourself, especially when this feels like such a big shift. What might it look like to remind yourself that this is just an experiment, not a pass-or-fail test?

client: I think reminding myself that it’s just an experiment could help, but it’s still hard to let go of that pass-or-fail mindset. I’ve always felt like I need to get things right the first time, or else I’m failing. Even framing it as an experiment feels like I’m setting myself up for disappointment if it doesn’t work out. It’s hard to trust that I’ll handle it well if things don’t go as planned.
therapist: It sounds like that "pass-or-fail" mindset runs deep—like even calling it an experiment doesn’t fully ease the fear of disappointment. That black-and-white thinking ("either I succeed or I fail") must feel exhausting to carry. What would it be like to notice, just for a moment, how much effort you're already putting into trying to get it *just right*?

client: It is exhausting—I’m constantly trying to anticipate every possible outcome so I don’t mess up. Even now, I’m overthinking this entire conversation, wondering if I’m doing therapy "right." It’s like I can’t turn off that part of my brain that’s always evaluating and judging everything I do. I don’t know how to let go of that, even for a moment.
therapist: I hear how draining it is to constantly monitor and judge yourself—even here, in a space meant to support you. That critical voice can feel relentless, always keeping you on high alert. What do you think might happen if, just for now, you let that voice simply *be there* without needing to obey it or fight it?
